title: In Psalms 63 In What Ways Does Remembering Gods Past Faithfulness Impact Our Current Faith And Worship
paragraphs: Remembering God’s Past Faithfulness: Lessons from Psalm 63

Psalm 63 is a beautiful expression of longing for God, written by David “when he was in the wilderness of Judah.” It is a psalm filled with vivid imagery, heartfelt devotion, and a deep confidence in God’s character. One of the striking features of this psalm is how David’s remembrance of God’s past faithfulness shapes his present faith and worship—even in the midst of hardship. Let’s explore how remembering what God has done in the past can profoundly impact our current walk with Him.
1. Remembrance Fuels Our Desire for God
David begins by expressing his deep thirst for God:
O God, thou art my God; earnestly will I seek thee: My soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee, In a dry and weary land, where no water is. - Psalm 63:1 ASV
His longing is not for deliverance alone, but for God Himself. This yearning is intensified by his recollection of previous encounters with God:
So have I looked upon thee in the sanctuary, To see thy power and thy glory. - Psalm 63:2 ASV

David remembers seeing God’s power and glory in the sanctuary. These memories nurture his present longing and give him hope that God is the same in the wilderness as He was in the sanctuary. Remembering God’s faithfulness in worship stirs up fresh desire and trust, even in barren seasons.
2. Remembrance Inspires Present Praise
David’s memory of God’s steadfast love leads him to praise, even in difficult circumstances:
Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, My lips shall praise thee. - Psalm 63:3 ASV

He makes a deliberate choice to worship God “so long as I live” (Psalm 63:4 ASV). This decision is rooted in his recollection of God’s unchanging love. When we remember how God has shown us mercy and kindness in the past, it compels us to praise Him in the present—no matter our circumstances.
3. Remembrance Sustains Us in the Night Seasons
David describes how he meditates on God during the night:
When I remember thee upon my bed, And meditate on thee in the night-watches. - Psalm 63:6 ASV

Nighttime can be a metaphor for seasons of anxiety or darkness. David’s habit of reflecting on God’s past help (“For thou hast been my help”—Psalm 63:7 ASV) gives him confidence and peace, enabling him to “rejoice in the shadow of thy wings.” When we recall God’s faithfulness during our past trials, it can calm our fears and strengthen our faith in the present.
4. Remembrance Strengthens Our Resolve to Cling to God
David confesses:
My soul followeth hard after thee: Thy right hand upholdeth me. - Psalm 63:8 ASV

His determination to cling to God is not merely self-effort; it’s rooted in his knowledge that God has upheld him before. Past experiences of God’s sustaining power give him assurance for the present and future. In times of weakness, remembering how God has held us up in the past encourages us to persevere in faith.
Biblical Patterns of Remembrance
Throughout Scripture, God commands His people to remember His works, as a safeguard against doubt and forgetfulness:
Remember his marvelous works that he hath done, His wonders, and the judgments of his mouth. - Psalm 105:5 ASV
Jesus instituted the Lord’s Supper as an act of remembrance (Luke 22:19 ASV), showing us that remembering God’s redemptive acts—supremely in Christ—should shape our worship and faith today.
Conclusion: The Power of Remembrance in Faith and Worship

Remembering God’s past faithfulness is not a nostalgic exercise, but a dynamic source of strength, praise, and perseverance in the present. As we meditate on God’s unchanging character and mighty deeds, our faith is renewed, our worship is deepened, and our hope is anchored in the God who “changes not” (Malachi 3:6 ASV). Let us, like David, cultivate the spiritual discipline of remembrance, allowing it to shape our response to God—no matter where we find ourselves today.
